div.head: Schedulability Analysis (SA) approaches that are based on a priori information and use fixed execution times with constant workloads work well in many application domains and allow pre-deployment guarantees of real-time performance such as Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA [2]
div.p: ). However, certain realtime applications must operate in highly dynamic environments, thereby precluding accurate characterization of workloads by static models. This leads to the notion that a new SA trigger for dynamic environments, in which applications experience large variations in the workload, needs to guarantee real-time performance during run-time. This paper examines the case of periodic, dynamic real-time systems, and describes an efficient SA policing technique which can trigger SA appropriately, and uses a dynamic threshold which becomes sensitive when the quality of service (QoS) of the dynamic real-time application approaches its deadline.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Schedulability Analysis (SA) approaches that are based on a priori Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) work well in many real-time application domains [1] and allow pre-deployment guarantees of performance. However, certain real-time applications must operate in highly dynamic environments, thereby precluding accurate characterization of the applications' workloads by static models. So execution times of applications in this paper are highly variable and unpredictableprior to run-time.

Thus, real-time operating systems in the dynamic environment should monitor system resources and workload changes and trigger reanalysis of schedulability appropriately. If SA Policing (SAP) introduced in [3] is overly sensitive, system overhead will be increased, and the system will be doing more work than necessary to guarantee real-time performance. Therefore, a novel, efficient SAP is desired to enable the system to be reliable without excess computation.

An important design decision in SAP techniques concerns the tradeoff of accuracy of SA vs. the overhead involved in achieving it. The triggering rate (the rate at which the SAP triggers reanalysis of schedulability) is the key variable. If SA is never triggered, this is equivalent to other offline approaches; at the other extreme, if SA is triggered frequently, the overhead becomes prohibitive. Thus, we have experimented with several triggering rates with both the Adaptive RMA (ARMA) and the Dynamic QoS Prediction (DQP) SA techniques functioning in the Dynamic SA (DSA) architecture depicted in Figure 1. The ARMA SA approach uses RMA with a posteriori execution time of an application rather than a priori WCET. The DQP SA tests performance of an application compared with QoS requirement (or deadline) during execution.

The results of DSA techniques will be applied to allocate or control resources dynamically by assessing QoS metrics and resource utilization metrics that are determined a posteriori. In our model, SA is invoked by SAP dynamically. Conditions in SAP are determined by the host and the application status, which can be monitored periodically by external monitors; the host monitor, the workload monitor and the performance monitor. That is, SAP should decide to trigger the SA request efficiently to justify schedulability of the realtime application. The system status parameters in our model include (1) workloads (denoted tl) of real-time application, 'A', (2) CPU Utilization Percentage (CUP) of a host, H k and (3) the Desired Control Level (DCL) of 'A' at current cycle, c.

div.p: We assume that a periodic real-time application 'A' is running on a host 'H k ' at cycle c with an amount of workload 'tl', execution time, C, and performance, λ. Thus, the DQP SA tests performance of an application such that λ λ λ λ(c) / λ λ λ λ req (A) ≤ ≤ ≤ ≤ 1, where λ req (A) is the QoS requirement (performance) of the application 'A'.
The remainder of this paper presents: dynamic DQP; SAP with Proportional, Integral, Derivative (PID) controller with experimental evaluations of the effectiveness of these techniques; and conclusion.

div.head: Probabilistic DQP
div.p: In this section, a DQP technique is presented. This approach, based on probabilistic techniques, is extended to be applicable to a time-sharing round-robin scheduler, which considers contention due to the same priority tasks and higher priority tasks (A*).

A new approach predicts the performance of 'A' (λ(A)), by considering periods (denoted as T) of applications to find contention among them. As introduced in [5] by Welch, Least Common Multiple (LCM) of periods of 'A' and 'A*' on H k is used in this approach. To extend this approach to round-robin scheduler, the execution time of 'A' (denoted as C) is analyzed in the unit of time quantum (TQ) and segment (S= C/TQ ). The TQ is defined by a function of priority levels. The following steps compute contention due to the same priority tasks to show to predict λ(A) (denoted as λ pred (A)). The priority of 'A' is denoted as p(A).
Step 1. Compute the resource requirement of 'A' (RS(A)) during the interval, [0,LCM].
Step 2. Compute the resource requirement of the other tasks (denoted as A*) during the interval, [0,LCM].
Step 3. Compute execution rate at which requests of 'A' are serviced.
Step 4. Compute utilization of the target and other tasks.

Step 5, a probabilistic execution rate (pr) considers (1) the probability of being with no usage of the resource (cp 0 (A)), (2) the chance that only 'A' uses the resource (cp 1 (A)), and (3) the chance that there is progress rate of 'A' within contention (cp 2 (A)).

div.head: Experiments of DQP with SAP
div.p: In this section experimental results are illustrated to measure accuracy of DQP and SAP. To generate the dynamic real-time environment, sensing applications in DynBench [7] are used and a filter application is used as a target task to predict response time. Results are shown in Figure 3 (a) using DQP with two different SA triggers, when tl changes by 1 and tl changes by 100. The results (L obs denoted as the observed QoS, which is response time) in both cases were similar. This indicates that a precise SA is not always necessary -it is almost as good to reevaluate SA when tl changes by 100 as when it changes by only 1; thus the overhead of dynamic SA can be reduced significantly if triggering is moderated. Figure 3 (b) shows the results when three SA triggers relating to changes in CUP by 1%, by 10% and 25%. In this case, the triggers of 1% and 10% performed reasonably, however, the 25% trigger performed poorly. Thus, it is not necessary to have SA performed for minute changes in CUP, because little (if any) accuracy is accrued for the additional intrusiveness required.

div.head: DSA with PID Controller
div.p: A feedback controller is designed to generate an output that causes some corrective effort to be applied so as to drive a measurable process variable towards a desired value known as the setpoint. Using a basic feedback controller, especially, Proportional, Integrated, Derivative (PID) controller, introduced in the Quasar scheduler [8], CPU proportion is reserved in a feedback manner. Our approach is to apply the PID controller to the QoS management of dynamic real-time applications over distributed computer clusters. In DeSiDeRaTa [9], there are QoS monitors and host resource monitors among middleware components. Especially, in [10], PID controller is explained well as follows: (1) the "Proportional" term causes a larger control action to be taken for a larger error; (2) the "Integral" term adds to the control action if the error has persisted for some time; and (3) the "Derivative" term supplements the control action if the error is changing rapidly with time.

The QoS of the process will be adjusted to the required QoS by the PID controller. The "QoS slack" denoted as "error" in Figure 5 will be reported every cycle.

div.head: Figure 5. PID controller mechanism
div.p: To find the proper level of of SA triggering, we carefully considers current error (denoted as e(k)), and all the previous errors ( e(k-1)), where k is current cycle of an application.
Fortunately, when the QoS is not changed significantly, the desired control level (b(k) or DCL) of an application also is not changed from the previous one (b(k-1)).

div.head: Dynamic Threshold of PID Controller
div.p: As we have seen with the problem of triggering SA, a threshold is required to reduce overhead of the SA module. When the threshold is fixed by any constant, it can be very sensitive SAP or not. It should cause the same tradeoff of the host load change or the workload change. Furthermore, the fixed threshold cannot adopt to dynamic system changes. For example, when current QoS approaches the requirement (set-point), we prefer to have a sensitive SAP to react to the environment.

Figure 6 shows how to compute the dynamic threshold, Threshold_PID(k). It is designed for reducing SA triggers and to be a sensitive SAP, when the DCL approaches the set-point (which means QoS slack becomes zero). From the formula (1), consider when the error changes are small (steady state), that is, e(k) ≅ e(k-1) ≅ e(k-2). If error changes are small, SAP may ignore the changes to trigger SA. To apply PID controller to the dynamic QoS management, DCL changes are carefully considered to trigger SA. Here, the DCL is not used as the target of the QoS to be reached. Therefore, from the The overall algorithm to trigger SA is explained in Figure 7. The main idea of the algorithm is "consulting with PID". If the DCL change from previous DCL is greater than the dynamic threshold, then trigger SA. Otherwise, ignore SA.

Figure 8 shows that a number of SA triggers with sensitive SAP such as 1% CPU change plus the dynamic threshold of PID controller are reduced by 33%. (An additional sensing applications in DynBench with fixed workload is running in background to impact the host load.)

The DSA technique which with 1% CPU change consulting with PID controller noted "CUP1%withPID" shown in Figure 9 performs accurately and appropriately (CUP obs denoted as the observed CPU utilization). The next experiment shown in Figure 10 illustrates the dynamic threshold that enables SA to be sensitive in order to trigger SA more frequently when current QoS approaches the QoS requirement, while the fixed threshold has no ability to reflect the system saturation.

The additional portion of "CUP1%withPID" from the shaded bar-graph of Figure 10 is the number of additional SA triggers with more restricted QoS constraint than the previous experiment. From this experiment, the dynamic threshold gains additional 25% sensitivity. Therefore, the designed threshold performs very well in terms of sensitvity and accuracy. It reduced many unnecessary SA triggers even though it uses very sensitive SAP strategy.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have developed two dynamic SA approaches for dynamic real-time systems, which provide adaptable RMA (ARMA) and dynamic QoS prediciton (DQP) on a round-robin time-sharing scheduler. We have identified engineering tradeoffs that must be made in the design of SA policing mechanisms, and have experimentally evaluated several SA policing implementations to show the importance of these tradeoffs.

Using PID controller, the dynamic threshold for PID controller reduced many unnecessary SA triggers, even though it uses very sensitive SAP strategy, such as 1% CPU change. Therefore, the designed threshold performs very well in terms of sensitvity and accuracy. It can be very effective method for the dynamic load balance. Finally, this paper identified that the design of the dynamic threshold is a very effective, necessary component through experiments with a dynamic realtime system testbed..
